# aeneid-077 drafter notes (X.439–509)

36 units. Title `Pallantis mors. Balteus`; part "The Death of Pallas (X.439–509)"; titleEn "The Death of Pallas —
Aeneid X.439–509". ¶ units: 439 only (Greenough's single paragraph start in this part). make_units.py prints no
warnings. `sc` not written.

## Misprints (rule 5b; t kept as printed, l/i corrected)
- **10.451 `minas. ”Fatus`** for `minas.” Fatus`. Handled as aeneid-075 (298, 335): unit 449–451 ends at `minas.`
  and its l/i close Pallas's speech with ”; the stray ” begins the t of unit 451 (`”Fatus medium procedit in aequor.`),
  whose l/i carry no mark. Note of 449 opens with the rule-5b sentence in 075's wording.
- **10.495 `hospitia. ”Et`** for `hospitia.” Et`. Same handling: unit 494–495 (`Haud illi… hospitia.`) closes Turnus's
  speech in l/i; the stray ” begins the t of unit 495–499 (5 lines, ending `auro;`), whose l/i carry no mark. Carrying
  the narrative on to `potitus.` (500) would have made 495–500 six lines, so the cut falls at `auro;` and 500 is its
  own unit. Note of 494 opens with the rule-5b sentence ("as at line 451").
- PAIRS = {449: 451, 494: 495}; mark balance is checked over each pair instead of unit by unit.
- No other misprint found (checked for lowercase after a stop, odd letters, misplaced marks). Kept as printed and not
  treated as misprints: 10.491 `“Arcades, haec, inquit,` (inquit inside the marks, Greenough's habit; noted);
  10.466 capital `Genitor` (Jupiter as a name); 10.492 `Euandro` (Greenough's Greek-style spelling; noted).
- 10.507 Greenough prints no comma after `parenti` (most editions punctuate `parenti, / haec te…`). Not a
  misprint that changes the sense; t as printed, the note says so in one clause.

## Half-line
- 10.490 `Quem Turnus super adsistens,` noted (unit 490–492) in the wording used for 284 in aeneid-075. Scanner

## Doubtful readings / variants
- Latin Library differences (siqua/si qua, nati/gnati, Adspice/aspice, volnere/vulnere, volnus/vulnus) are all
  orthographic; none noted as variants. Greenough's spellings explained once: siqua, Adspice, mage, volnus,
  adsis, adfatur, adsistens, inreparabile, reicit, baltei (two syllables), biiugis (pointer to 400).
- 10.473 `oculos Rutulorum reicit arvis`: taken as "turns his eyes away from the fields" (arvis ablative of
  separation); the note mentions the alternative (dative, "turns his eyes back to the field"). I am not sure which
  Conington/Greenough prefer; reviewer may want to check.
- 10.445–448 `iussa superba miratus` taken as object of miratus; `stupet in Turno` "is amazed at Turnus".
- 10.478 `strinxit` with the object left unexpressed ("grazed"), the usual reading.
- 10.439 `soror alma` identified in n as Juturna (named only later, Book XII).

## Famous lines not on the set-piece list
- 10.467–469 *Stat sua cuique dies… hoc virtutis opus*: i "Every man has his appointed day; for all men the span of
  life is short, and once gone it can never be restored; but to make one's name outlast one by what one does, that is
  what courage is for." Drafted from the Latin; checked against memory of familiar English versions; no distinctive
  verbatim echo that I can detect (avoided "irretrievable/irrecoverable" stock phrasing in i).
- 10.501–502 *Nescia mens hominum fati sortisque futurae…*: i "How blind the minds of men are to fate and to what
  lies ahead, and how unable to keep within bounds when good fortune raises them high!" Same check; avoided the
  common "ignorant of fate… future lot" wording in i (l keeps the literal "Ignorant… of fate and of lot to come",
  which is the bare gloss of the Latin).
- Should either become a house rendering? Not proposed.

## Attributions written from memory, not checked against a text
- Lion and bull simile at Sarpedon's death, Iliad 16.487–489.
- Zeus weeps tears of blood for Sarpedon, Iliad 16.459–461; Zeus and Hera on saving Sarpedon, Iliad 16.431–461.
- Patroclus's heel on Sarpedon's chest to draw his spear, Iliad 16.503–504.
- Hector's spear through six of the seven layers of Ajax's shield, Iliad 7.245–248.
- "his armour rang upon him", Iliad 4.504 and often; "bit the earth", Iliad 2.418, 11.749.
- Zeus pities Hector putting on Achilles' armour, Iliad 17.198–208.
- Aeneas `premit altum corde dolorem`, I.209; Turnus killed for the belt, XII.940–952.
- Hercules, Cacus and Evander's welcome (Book VIII, no line given); Hercules as grandson of Alcaeus; Danaids
  (fifty daughters of Danaus, sons of Aegyptus); spolia opima definition; Clonus son of Eurytus known only here.
- "More than fifty" half-lines (as in 075).

## Decisions
- Advisory: none. `claude/content-advisory.md` is not in this checkout (no `claude/` folder at the repo root; also
  recorded in QUESTIONS items 36 and 40). Pallas's death is ordinary battle killing (conventions; item 61 practice).
  The belt's scene is the Danaids' murder of their bridegrooms on the wedding night: killing, not sexual violence,
  told in one line; no trigger applies.
- 453–456 split at `comminus;` so the lion simile stands as its own unit; 490–492 split at `Euandro;`.
- No new house renderings; new-renderings.md says "None."
